draft.title: Contention and supporting arguments
card: Contention
the main point a writer argues. It is a claim that someone could disagree with, and the whole piece works to prove it.
Supporting argument
a reason the contention is true. Each one usually gets its own paragraph.
Evidence
a fact, statistic, example or expert view that backs up a supporting argument. A reason with no evidence is only an opinion.
Example: "Schools should start later." Reason: teenagers need more sleep. Evidence: a survey of tired students. Each reason points back to the contention.
draft.remember: The contention is the claim. Reasons support it, and evidence backs each reason.

a.q: Which sentence is the contention of a persuasive article?
opts: Our town should build a skate park for young people
Skate parks are usually made of concrete and steel
The council opened a new library in the town last year
A survey found that many local teens skate each week
a.why: The first option is a claim that someone could disagree with, and a writer could argue it. The survey result is tempting, but it is evidence that supports a claim, not the main point itself.
a.clue: Which sentence is a claim a reader might disagree with?

b.q: Priya argues that "Students should learn to cook at school." Which sentence is a supporting argument with evidence?
opts: Cooking builds health: a survey found cooks eat more veg
Cooking is a topic that many people like to talk about
Many students enjoy food, so schools should think about it
Students should learn cooking because it is a good idea
b.why: The first option gives a reason (cooking builds health) and evidence (a survey). The last option only repeats the contention with the word because, so it gives no real reason or evidence.
b.clue: Look for a reason plus a fact that backs it up.

a.best: Our town should build a skate park for young people

b.best: Cooking builds health: a survey found cooks eat more veg

problems.detail: Why (a) names the answer by position ('The first option is a claim'). Options are shown in random order, so here the first option is the survey sentence, which the why then calls evidence. This contradicts itself for the student. Name the option by its words instead.

Why (b) refers to 'the first option' and 'the last option'. In the shuffled order, the last option is 'Cooking is a topic...', not the 'because' sentence the why describes. Refer to options by their content, not their position.

check.summary: The card and both questions are correct and suit Year 9. Both explanations refer to options by position ('first', 'last'), which won't match the shuffled order students see, so they should quote the option instead.
